newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico rows back on petrochemical sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Mexico rows back on petrochemical sell-off.

text.p: Bowing to stiff political pressure, Mexico on Sunday scrapped a four-year-old project to end its control of the cash-strapped petrochemical industry, and offered to go halves with the private sector instead.

In one of the most significant policy reversals during the administration of President Ernesto Zedillo, Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles acknowledged that the privatisation of 61 secondary petrochemical firms had stalled.
"The programme has gone much more slowly than we desired," he told a news conference.

Faced by stubborn opposition from within the ranks of its own ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party and Mexico's powerful oil workers union, as well as many other sectors of society, the government, he said, had changed tack.

Instead of fully privatising those plants that produce materials the government considered non-strategic, he said, state oil firm Petroleos Mexicanos, known as Pemex, would retain at least a 51 percent stake in each plant.

In perhaps 10 to 15 units where there is likely to be strong demand, the government planned to allow domestic and foreign investors to take a 49 percent stake, which they would acquire by building onto existing structures to boost capacity.
Also, Mexico will encourage investors to set up new plants in which they would have 100 percent ownership.

The sale of the first unit put onto the auction block last April, Cosoleacaque, was cancelled, Reyes Heroles said. He added that Energy Ministry officials were in talks on Sunday with the bidders in that auction to explain the decision.
He did not expect any private sector participation in the Pemex plants under the new scheme until the second half of next year.

Opposition to the petrochemical sell-off, he said, underscored the political difficulties of meddling with Mexico's jealously protected oil industry, nationalised in 1938 in one of Mexico's proudest moments of the 20th century.
But he also cast the move as evidence that the government was prepared to listen to criticism, and respond to it with constructive alternatives.

Bickering over the privatisation had put off potential investors in the cash-strapped industry, and Reyes Heroles said there was some $5 billion in potential investments waiting to come in when conditions were right.

He also announced a move that would give more legal security to potential participants in the industry, saying the government would send to Congress a bill defining in the Constitution nine strategic petrochemicals that only Pemex has the right to exploit.
